impact.location_description: Mid-Atlantic Ocean, roughly 1,450 km northeast of French Guiana; predicted uncertainty corridor spanned from Central America to East Africa before infrasound narrowed it
impact.context: Deep open ocean, far from any landmass or shipping; no optical, satellite, or radar detection of any kind.

sensor_detections: Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) International Monitoring System infrasound, 3 stations
confirmation.eyewitness: None; no optical, satellite-flash, or radar detection was ever obtained -- infrasound is the sole evidence base.

scientific_results: 2014 AA is the only one of the 13 cases confirmed exclusively by ground-based infrasound triangulation, with zero optical, satellite-sensor, or eyewitness corroboration -- a methodological first that demonstrated CTBTO's nuclear-test-monitoring network could double as a NEO-impact confirmation tool.

Farnocchia, Chesley, Brown & Chodas (2016, Icarus) combined the sparse 7-point, 69-minute optical arc with the infrasound-derived impact time/location in a joint least-squares fit, substantially refining both the pre-impact orbit and the impact location beyond what either data source gave alone.

de la Fuente Marcos et al. (2016, Astrophysics & Space Science) independently re-derived impact parameters and explored the pre-impact orbital evolution, cross-checking the Farnocchia et al. solution.

As the very first case where an impact was confirmed with no fireball imagery at all, 2014 AA established the analytical template (arc + external timing constraint) later reused for 2019 MO and 2024 UQ.

notable_papers.authors: Farnocchia, D., Chesley, S. R., Brown, P. G., Chodas, P. W.
notable_papers.topic: The trajectory and atmospheric impact of asteroid 2014 AA

notable_papers.authors: de la Fuente Marcos, C., de la Fuente Marcos, R., et al.
notable_papers.topic: Homing in for New Year: impact parameters and pre-impact orbital evolution of meteoroid 2014 AA

narrative: Richard Kowalski discovered 2014 AA with the Mount Lemmon telescope at 06:18 UTC on 1 January 2014, obtaining just seven positions over 69 minutes before the object faded from view -- too short an arc to pin down anything but a wide impact corridor stretching from Central America to East Africa. No fireball, satellite flash, or eyewitness report ever surfaced; the only confirming evidence came about a day later, when three CTBTO infrasound stations recorded a signal consistent with an atmospheric explosion over the open Atlantic, roughly 1,450 km northeast of French Guiana, about 20.8 hours after discovery. Two independent groups (Farnocchia et al. 2016; de la Fuente Marcos et al. 2016) later combined the sparse optical astrometry with the infrasound timing to refine the object's orbit and impact parameters, establishing that a hazardous-sized object had struck Earth with confirmation resting on treaty-monitoring instruments never designed for astronomy. It remains the only one of the 13 cases with no optical or satellite detection of the impact itself.
